html:
Rust's pitch is "fearless concurrency": data races are a compile error, not a production incident. This module covers threads, channels, shared state, and the two marker traits that make it all work.

Send and Sync

Two auto-traits. You almost never implement them; you do need to read them in error messages.

  • T: Send — a T can be moved to another thread.
  • T: Sync — a &T can be shared between threads.

Rc<T> is neither Send nor Sync (its counter is not atomic). Arc<T> is both, when T: Send + Sync. RefCell<T> is Send but not Sync. Mutex<T> is both, when T: Send.

Type Send Sync
i32, String, Vec<T> (if T) yes yes
Rc<T> no no
Arc<T> if T: Send + Sync if T: Send + Sync
RefCell<T> if T: Send no
Mutex<T> if T: Send if T: Send
Cell<T> if T: Send no
raw pointers no no

Scoped threads — borrow without Arc

thread::scope (stable since 1.63) removes the need for Arc in the common "parallel loop over borrowed data" case. Prefer it.

Channels

Message passing: no shared state, no locks.

mpsc = multi-producer, single-consumer. For work queues you usually want the crossbeam or flume crate, or tokio::sync::mpsc in async code.

Bounded channels apply backpressure

An unbounded channel in a producer-faster-than-consumer pipeline is a memory leak with extra steps. Bound it.

Shared state

Gotcha: holding a MutexGuard across a long operation serialises everything. Copy the values you need out, drop the guard, then do the work:

Deadlock: the lock-ordering problem

Fixes, in order of preference: never hold two locks at once; if you must, always acquire in a documented global order; or use try_lock with a timeout.

Parallelism with rayon

For CPU-bound work over a collection, rayon is the shortest path. It uses a work-stealing pool and turns .iter() into .par_iter().

Rule: parallelise the outermost loop only. Nested par_iter causes oversubscription.

Parallel map-reduce with a thread pool

This is what rayon does internally, minus the cleverness. Writing it once by hand is worth it for understanding work stealing.

When to use threads vs async

Workload Use
CPU-bound, parallelisable over data rayon / threads
Many I/O waits (network, disk) async (module 02.11)
A fixed set of long-running tasks threads
Thousands of concurrent connections async
Simple background job, no I/O thread

Async does not make CPU work faster — it multiplexes waiting. Doing CPU work inside an async task blocks the executor and starves every other task on that worker thread.

A worked example: a bounded worker pool

Two details that matter: the MutexGuard is scoped so the lock is not held while the job runs (otherwise it is a single-threaded pool), and Drop closes the channel so workers exit rather than blocking forever.

Exercises

  1. Spawn 10 threads that each increment a shared AtomicUsize 1000 times. Assert the total.
  2. Build a producer/consumer pair with a bounded sync_channel(4) and observe the backpressure with timing prints.
  3. Rewrite a Vec-summing loop with rayon::par_iter() and compare wall time on 10M elements.
  4. Use thread::scope to sort four slices of one &mut Vec in parallel with split_at_mut.
  5. Deliberately create a deadlock with two mutexes, then fix it with a consistent lock order.
  6. Explain the compiler error you get when you try to move an Rc<T> into a thread::spawn closure.
